turns.doctor_question: Hi, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?
turns.patient_response:
Well, it's... I guess I'm here because things at my apartment have just gotten completely out of hand. I live over in this complex, and you know, you get to know the rhythms of a place when you're around all day. You know who is supposed to be where. But lately... well, I know for a fact that the people in my building are watching me. They are keeping track of all my comings and goings. Every time I open my front door, I hear a deadbolt click, or I see somebody's blinds twitching out of the corner of my eye. 

And they're not just watching, they're actually slipping notes about me to the management office. I've seen them sneaking around the hallways with these pieces of paper. I try to mind my own business, I keep my TV turned down low, I don't bother a single soul, but they are constantly reporting on me. 

And the thing that really drives me crazy—and I guess why I was told I needed to come talk to you—is that everybody keeps telling me it's just regular notices on the doors. The property manager, my family, they all try to brush it off and tell me, "Oh, it's just flyers for pest control," or "They're just taping up water shut-off notices." But I know what I'm looking at. I know they're writing things down about exactly when I leave for the store and when I come back, and it's just... it's exhausting, honestly, having to look over your shoulder every single time you just want to step outside to check the mail.

symptom_reasoning.S019: The patient describes a fixed belief that neighbors are watching them and reporting on them to management, which they maintain despite contradictory evidence and reassurances from family and the property manager.

top_partial.disease_name: Bipolar I Disorder with Psychotic Features

turns.doctor_question: Have you been hearing voices when no one is there?
turns.patient_response:
Voices? No, no, it's not like that. I'm not... I don't hear things that aren't there, if that's what you're asking. I mean, I hear *people* talking, but they are real people. You know how these apartment buildings are, especially the older ones like mine. They must have built this place thirty, forty years ago, and they didn't put a lick of insulation between the drywall. 

So, if somebody is out in the hallway, or lingering by the stairwell—which they do, constantly—I can hear them mumbling. I can hear them whispering to each other. I can't always make out every single word, but I know it's them coordinating their little shifts, talking about what I'm doing. But it's not voices in my head or anything like that. It's just the actual neighbors. The guy in 2B, or that woman who walks her dog at all hours. 

I hear the floorboards creaking under the cheap carpet out there. I hear the tape ripping when they stick those notes on the doors. I hear the deadbolts. I just sit in my living room, completely quiet, sometimes for hours with the TV on mute, and I just listen to it all. And you wouldn't believe the amount of rustling and whispering that goes on right outside my door if you really pay attention. So I hear all of that, yes, but not... not ghosts or imaginary voices, no. Just the people who won't leave me be.

symptom_reasoning.S019: The patient expresses a fixed belief that neighbors are coordinating shifts and whispering about them, indicating persecutory delusions.
symptom_reasoning.S020: The patient explicitly denies hearing imaginary voices or things that are not there.

turns.doctor_question: Have you had the feeling that someone else is putting thoughts into your mind or controlling your thoughts?
turns.patient_response:
Controlling my thoughts? No, no, nothing like that. My thoughts are my own. I mean, they can watch me all they want out there, they can write down every little thing I do and slip their little notes around to the management, but they can't get inside my head. 

I've got a lot of time to think, you know, not working and just being stuck in that apartment most of the day. I do a whole lot of thinking. I sit there on the couch, TV muted like I said, and I just turn things over in my mind. I think about how things used to be before this whole complex went downhill, or I try to figure out the patterns of what the neighbors are doing. But nobody is putting those thoughts in there. It's just me. 

I've always had a strong mind, always knew my own mind, even back when I was younger. I might not have finished high school, but I'm not stupid, and I know the difference between my own thoughts and... well, whatever else. So if you're asking if they have some kind of way to beam things into my brain, or if they're pulling strings in my head like a puppet? No. They're just sneaky people out in the hallway. I have to use my own brain to try and stay one step ahead of them, honestly. It takes a lot of mental energy to keep track of it all, trying to piece together why they're so interested in me, but it's all my own doing. Nobody's controlling what's up here but me.

symptom_reasoning.S019: The patient explicitly describes persecutory delusions, expressing a fixed belief that neighbors are constantly watching them, taking notes on their activities, and reporting them to management.

turns.doctor_question: Have there been times when you felt unusually energetic and needed much less sleep than usual?
turns.patient_response:
Energetic? Lord, no. I don't think I've felt energetic since... well, I can't even remember. It feels like years. Honestly, most days it's exactly the opposite. It's like I'm walking through molasses. Getting off the couch just to go to the kitchen and pour a glass of water feels like this massive undertaking. I just sit there. 

And as for sleep... well, I sleep all the time, really. Or at least, I try to. I'll lay down in the afternoon because I'm just so completely drained, physically and mentally drained from just existing in that apartment and listening to the hallway. I'll pull the blanket up, even if it's two o'clock in the afternoon, and I'll just stay there. Sometimes I sleep, sometimes I just lay there staring at the ceiling fan because I don't have the energy to do anything else. 

I've never had a time where I felt like I could just go and go and go without resting. I know some people get like that, my brother used to be able to work a double shift and then go fishing, but not me. I need my sleep. And lately, it feels like no matter how much I sleep, I wake up just as tired. It's a heavy kind of tired, you know? Like it's settled right into my bones. So, no, definitely not unusually energetic. Not even a little bit. I'd give anything for just a fraction of some energy, just enough to maybe clean the kitchen counters, but it's just not there.

turns.doctor_question: How long have you been feeling that your neighbors are watching you and reporting on you?
turns.patient_response:
Well, let me think on that. It’s... it hasn't been forever, but when you're sitting in it every single day, it sure feels like a lifetime. If I had to put a strict timeline on it, I’d say it’s been about a year and a month now. Yeah, right around thirteen months. 

I know that because it was exactly when the building got bought out and they brought in that new management company for the front office. Before that, nobody cared what you did. You kept to yourself, they kept to themselves. But then this new office staff comes in, and suddenly there are all these new rules, new notices taped to everyone's doors every other week. And that’s exactly when I started noticing the neighbors acting strange. It was like the office put them up to it, you know? Like they told them to keep an eye on the older guy who's home all day. 

I remember it was a year and a month ago when I first caught that guy in 2B just lingering right outside my door. He made some excuse, muttered something and pretended he was looking through his pockets for his mail key, but you don't stand there in dead silence for five minutes looking for a key. And ever since that specific day, it’s just been constant. A year and a month of them watching when I take my trash out, watching when I check the mail, listening through the drywall. 

I know they’re reporting everything back to the office. The office probably wants to find a reason to kick me out so they can put down some cheap laminate flooring and charge double the rent to some younger folks. That's how these places work, I've seen it happen. So they have the neighbors doing their dirty work, keeping tabs on me, slipping their little reports to the manager. It’s exhausting, it really is, dealing with this for over a year. You’d think they would get bored of watching a tired old man sit on his couch, but no, thirteen months of this nonsense and they're still at it, day and night.

symptom_reasoning.S019: The patient expresses a fixed, persecutory belief that his neighbors are constantly watching him, listening through the walls, and reporting to the management office to get him evicted.

turns.doctor_question: Have you lost interest in things you used to enjoy?
turns.patient_response:
Lost interest? Yeah, I'd say so. I'd say I've lost interest in just about everything, honestly. It's funny you ask that, because I was just thinking the other day about how different my Sundays used to be. I used to have a whole routine, you know? A whole schedule. I used to really look forward to choir practice. I'm not the best singer in the world, mind you, but I liked being part of it, the harmony, all those voices coming together. And then after choir, there was bridge. We had a regular group, four of us, and we'd play for hours. We weren't playing for money or anything, just bragging rights, but it was... it was nice. It felt good to use my brain like that, strategizing, trying to figure out what cards the others were holding. 

And cooking, too. I used to love making this big pot of beans every Sunday. My grandmother's recipe, with the ham hock and the onions, letting it simmer all day so the whole apartment smelled like it. I'd make enough to last me half the week. I even used to do little repair jobs for folks around the building, you know? Fixing a leaky faucet, tightening up a loose cabinet hinge. I liked feeling useful. I liked working with my hands. 

But now? Now I don't do any of it. None of it. The choir director called a few times, left messages, but I just let the phone ring. I sit there on the couch and watch it ring, and I just tell myself there's no point in going. There's just no point. The bridge group probably found a replacement by now, and I haven't cooked those beans in months. The thought of chopping the onions, standing over the stove... it's just too much. I don't have it in me. And I certainly don't want to be going into anyone else's apartment to fix their cabinets when I know half of them are the ones whispering about me to the management. Why would I help them? But even if they weren't, I just... I don't care anymore. The things that used to bring me a little bit of joy, a little bit of satisfaction, they just feel empty now. It's like all the color drained out of them, and I'm just left sitting here in the gray, waiting for the day to be over. So, yes, I've lost interest. Completely.

symptom_reasoning.S019: The patient expresses a persecutory belief that neighbors are whispering about them to the management.
symptom_reasoning.S024: The patient describes feeling empty and sitting in the 'gray' waiting for the day to end, indicating a depressed and empty mood.
symptom_reasoning.S025: The patient explicitly confirms losing interest in all previously enjoyed activities, such as choir, bridge, and cooking.
symptom_reasoning.S029: The patient notes that the thought of cooking is 'too much' and they 'don't have it in me,' indicating a marked loss of energy.

turns.doctor_question: Have you been feeling this down and uninterested nearly every day for at least two weeks?
turns.patient_response:
Two weeks? Oh, Lord, if it was only two weeks, I’d count my blessings. Two weeks is just a bad mood or a rough patch. No, doc, it’s been way, way longer than that. If I really sit and trace it back... it's been about a year and two months. Yeah, a year and two months of this. 

I know because, like I was saying before about the building management changing a year and a month ago? Well, this heavy, no-point feeling started just a little bit before all that mess even kicked off. I was already starting to pull away from things right before they put those first notices on the doors. So it’s been a year and two months of just... nothing. Every single day. You wake up, and before your eyes are even fully open, that heavy feeling is just sitting right there on your chest. And you think to yourself, what is the point? Why get up? Why make a pot of coffee? Why go out and talk to anybody? 

It’s a terrible thing, pulling away from things you used to care about, and you don't even really make a conscious choice to do it. It just happens because you don't have the strength to fight that no-point feeling anymore. A year and two months is a long time to sit on a couch, let me tell you. You watch the sun come up, you watch it go down, and it's just one long, continuous stretch of gray. I used to try to keep track of the days, but after a while, you just stop, because a Tuesday feels exactly like a Saturday. I haven't had a single day in all those fourteen months where I woke up and thought, hey, today's the day I'm gonna get back out there and go to choir. Not one. 

So, no, not two weeks. A year and two months of feeling completely hollowed out and heavy all at the exact same time. I don't know how else to explain it, but it's every single day, without fail, from the minute I open my eyes to the minute I finally manage to get back to sleep.

symptom_reasoning.S024: The patient describes a persistent 'heavy' feeling and feeling 'completely hollowed out' every single day for over a year.
symptom_reasoning.S025: The patient reports 'pulling away from things you used to care about' and no longer having the motivation to go to choir.
symptom_reasoning.S083: The patient expresses a profound sense of pointlessness, repeatedly asking 'what is the point?' and describing a 'no-point feeling'.

turns.doctor_question: During this past year, was there ever a period of at least two weeks when you felt this down even though the neighbors were not watching or reporting on you?
turns.patient_response:
Well, see, the thing about that is... you've got it a little backwards, doc. If you're asking if they ever took a break from watching me, the answer is absolutely not. They never stopped. Not for one single day, not for a weekend, not for a holiday. 

But... if I really sit and think about it, there actually was a short little stretch in the middle of all this. Just a spell of several weeks, maybe a few months ago, where I actually felt a little bit of a shift in myself. I remember it clearly because I was actually eating a bit better for a minute there. I had gone down to the little market on the corner and bought some actual food—some sliced turkey, a loaf of bread, some real cheese—instead of just sitting on the couch eating stale saltines out of the box. I was making myself actual sandwiches. And I noticed I wasn't waking up feeling quite so hopeless, either. For those few weeks, I’d open my eyes in the morning and that heavy, gray, what's-the-point feeling wasn't pressing down on my chest quite so hard. I actually thought to myself, well, maybe I'm finally catching a break from feeling so utterly miserable. 

But here's the kicker. Even then, even when I was eating my sandwiches and waking up with a little more fight in me, I still knew exactly what was happening out in that hallway. I'd be sitting there at my little kitchen table, feeling a bit lighter, but I still believed—no, I knew for a fact—that the neighbors were out there watching my door. I could feel them doing it. I knew they were still keeping their logs, still reporting every little noise I made right back to the management office. 

So, I might have had a few weeks where the depression backed off just a tiny bit and let me breathe, but the watching? The reporting? That never stopped. Not for a second. Even when I was feeling a little better, I was still a target to them. They just don't ever quit.

symptom_reasoning.S019: The patient expresses a fixed, persecutory belief that neighbors are constantly watching their door and reporting on them.
symptom_reasoning.S024: The patient describes usually having a 'heavy, gray, what's-the-point feeling' pressing down on their chest, indicating a persistent depressed mood.
symptom_reasoning.S026: The patient mentions usually 'just sitting on the couch eating stale saltines', indicating a significant decrease in appetite outside of their brief period of improvement.

turns.doctor_question: Was there ever a period of at least two weeks when you still believed your neighbors were watching and reporting on you, but you were not feeling depressed?
turns.patient_response:
Yeah, exactly. That's... that's just what I was trying to explain to you a second ago, doc. Like I said, there was this spell... a spell of several weeks, maybe a month or two back. It’s hard to keep the exact dates straight when you're cooped up in an apartment all day, but it was definitely a good few weeks where things felt different inside my own head. I was actually eating a bit better, like I mentioned with the deli meat and the real cheese. Provolone, I think it was. Or maybe Swiss, I can't quite recall. But the point is, I was taking care of myself a little bit more, and I wasn't waking up feeling so completely hopeless and heavy every single morning. I could actually breathe a little easier. 

But—and this is the thing you really gotta understand—even during those few weeks when that heavy feeling took a little vacation, I still believed... well, I didn't just believe, I knew for a fact... that the neighbors were watching my door. I'd be sitting there at my little table, chewing my sandwich, feeling alright for a change, but my eyes would be glued to the crack under the front door. Because I knew they were out in that hallway. I knew they were still keeping their little logs and reporting every little thing I did to the building manager. 

The sadness might have given me a break for those several weeks, sure. I wasn't waking up with that terrible dread. But those people? They never gave me a break. So, yes, to answer your question, there was a period of a few weeks where I wasn't feeling so down, but I absolutely still knew they were watching and reporting on me the whole time.

symptom_reasoning.S019: The patient expresses a fixed, certain belief that their neighbors are watching their door and reporting on them.

turns.doctor_question: Aside from feeling depressed, have you had a long period where it was hard to speak much or show emotion, even when talking with other people?
turns.patient_response:
No, no, I wouldn't say that. I mean, I can talk just fine when I need to. Well, when there's actually someone to talk to, which isn't often these days, what with me staying inside all the time. But when I do talk, like right now with you, I don't have any trouble getting the words out or showing how I feel about things. 

If anything, my problem is usually the opposite, doc. Once I get going, especially if I'm upset about something, like those notices on my door or the way the neighbors are always lurking around, I can get pretty worked up. My voice gets loud, my hands start shaking, I can feel my heart just hammering away in my chest. You can definitely tell exactly how I'm feeling when that happens. There's no hiding it. 

I remember this one time, oh, it must have been a few months back, right before that little spell where I was eating better. I had to call the management office because they’d left another one of those vague, threatening notes slipped under my door. I was so angry, so just... fed up with the whole situation, that I was practically shouting into the phone. The lady on the other end kept telling me to calm down, but I couldn't. I was pacing the floor, waving my arms around like a madman, even though she couldn't see me. I was just so full of emotion, you know? It was all pouring out of me. 

So, no, I've never had a time where I couldn't speak or show emotion. If I'm feeling something, whether it's that heavy, gray sadness or that hot, burning anger about being spied on, it shows. It definitely shows. Sometimes I wish I could just turn it off, just be blank and not feel anything at all, but that's just not how I'm wired, I guess. The feelings are always right there, right on the surface, ready to spill over the second I open my mouth.

turns.doctor_question: Was there ever a full month when you still knew your neighbors were watching and reporting on you, but you were not feeling depressed?
turns.patient_response:
Doc, I feel like we're going in circles a little bit here. Like I was just saying a minute ago with the whole sandwich thing... you're asking if it was exactly a full month now. 

See, the thing is, when you don't have a job to go to—which I haven't for a good long while now, just living on what I can get by on—and you're just sitting in the exact same apartment day in and day out, the days just sort of bleed into one another. Monday feels like Thursday, Sunday feels like Tuesday. You lose track of the calendar when there's nowhere you have to be. 

So, if you're pinning me down and asking if it was exactly thirty days, a whole calendar month... I can't swear to it on a stack of Bibles. What I do know, like I was just trying to explain, is that there was definitely a spell of several weeks. Could have been three weeks, could have been five, I really couldn't tell you the exact math on it. But for those several weeks, I was eating a bit better, making those real meals instead of eating stale crackers, and I wasn't waking up feeling so completely hopeless and weighed down by everything. 

But as for the rest of it? The spying? That never stopped. Not for a day, let alone a month. Even when that heavy sadness lifted for those several weeks, I still believed—I knew for an absolute fact—that the neighbors were watching my door and reporting on me. I'd be chewing my food, feeling alright for once, but my eyes were still locked on that hallway. So, several weeks, yes, absolutely. But I couldn't tell you if it crossed the finish line into a full month. All I know is the mood got better for a spell, but the neighbors never quit.

turns.doctor_question: Have you ever felt that ordinary things around you—like TV shows, radio, or strangers’ comments—were sending special messages meant specifically for you?
turns.patient_response:
No, no, nothing like that. I mean, I watch TV, sure. Mostly the old reruns, you know? The stuff from the seventies and eighties, back when things made a little more sense. The comedies, mostly. M*A*S*H, Barney Miller, that sort of thing. I'll just leave it on in the background while I'm sitting at the table, just to have some noise in the apartment so it's not so dead quiet all the time. But it's just a TV show. Hawkeye Pierce isn't trying to talk to me through the screen, if that's what you're asking. 

And the radio... well, I don't really listen to the radio much anymore. Used to, back when I had a car, I'd listen to the classic rock stations, maybe a little talk radio if the music was no good. But in the apartment, it's just the TV. And strangers? Like I said, I don't go out much. I stay inside. So there aren't any strangers around to make comments, special messages or otherwise. 

The only people sending messages are the neighbors, and they aren't using the TV to do it. They're just writing down everything I do and slipping those vague little notes under my door. That's real. That's actually happening right outside my living room. But the TV? The radio? No, they're just... they're just boxes making noise. They don't know who I am, and they certainly aren't trying to send me any secret codes or anything crazy like that. I'm just a guy sitting in his apartment, trying to get by, trying to keep an eye on the door. That's all.

symptom_reasoning.S019: The patient denies referential delusions regarding the TV or radio, but clearly expresses persecutory delusions by claiming his neighbors are surveilling him and slipping notes under his door.
symptom_reasoning.S079: The patient describes a state of sustained alertness and safety checking, noting that he stays inside and is 'trying to keep an eye on the door.'

turns.doctor_question: Have you ever seen something that other people could not see?
turns.patient_response:
See things? Like... like visions or something? No, no, definitely not. I mean, my eyes aren't exactly what they used to be, I'll give you that. I'm fifty-nine now, and... well, things get a little fuzzy around the edges sometimes. I actually had to go down to the pharmacy a couple years back and buy one of those cheap pairs of reading glasses off the little spinning rack they have near the register. Just the plastic ones, you know? Because I was having trouble making out the small print on the back of the soup cans and the cracker boxes. And, of course, I have to put them on to read those damn notes the neighbors keep sliding under my door. 

But as far as seeing things that aren't actually there, like... I don't know, ghosts or imaginary people? No, never anything like that. If I see it, it's really there. Like the shadows under the door crack. When they're standing out there in the hall, just waiting and listening, I can see their shadow blocking the light from the hallway. I see that plain as day. Sometimes I'll sit there in the armchair for... oh, it feels like hours, just staring at that little gap between the bottom of the door and the linoleum, just waiting for the shadow to shift. But that's a real shadow, from a real person who's actually out there spying on me. It's not some trick of the light or my mind playing games with me. 

So, no, besides just needing those cheap glasses to read, my eyes only show me what's really in the room with me. Just the old furniture, the TV, and the door. Always the door. I've never seen anything that someone else wouldn't see if they were sitting right there next to me.

symptom_reasoning.S019: The patient expresses a fixed, paranoid belief that neighbors are spying on them and standing outside their door listening.

Doc, I... I feel like we're just spinning our wheels here, going over the exact same ground we just covered. Didn't you just ask me this? I could swear you just asked me this exact same thing about five minutes ago.

turns.doctor_question: Has anyone told you that your speech or behavior became very disorganized or hard to follow?
turns.patient_response:
Well, I mean, people don't talk to me much these days, mostly because I don't give them the chance. But... well, yeah, I guess there have been a few times. The guy at the corner store, for one. I went down there a while back, maybe a couple months ago, just to get some milk and maybe a loaf of bread, you know, the basics. And I was trying to explain to him why I needed him to double-bag the groceries, because I didn't want the bottoms falling out on the stairs, and somehow I got to talking about the rent. 

Because the rent, you see, they raised it again, and it's just getting impossible on what I have coming in. So I'm talking about the rent, and then I remembered this time back when I used to go down to the marina, just to watch the boats, back before things got so bad. I was telling the clerk about the marina, and the boats, and then... well, I don't know how I got there, but I started talking about choir robes. My aunt used to sing in a choir, had these big heavy maroon robes, and I was trying to explain how the fabric felt, because it reminded me of something, maybe the curtains in the apartment. 

And then, of course, I had to mention the wires in the walls, because that's the real problem, isn't it? The wires they use to listen in. I was trying to explain how the wires connect everything, how they run right behind the plaster where you can't see them but you know they're there. And I'm trying to lay it all out for him, making the connections—the rent, the marina, the robes, the wires—and he just... he just stared at me. He had this look on his face, like his eyes were glazed over, and he said, "Buddy, I don't know what you're talking about, just take your groceries."

'Please remit payment by...' or 'Your upcoming appointment is...' I read the words, and I know they're English, but they just don't mean anything. They don't stick together in my head. And then I'll have a bill in one hand, and maybe a clinic card in the other, and I just stare at them because I completely lose the ability to figure out what to do. I just can't decide what needs doing first. Which one is more important? Do I pay this? Do I call them? Do I need to find a stamp? 

My thoughts just get all tangled up, like a bird's nest of old fishing line. I'll sit there for twenty, thirty minutes, just reading that exact same sentence about the balance due, trying to force my brain to make a simple decision, but it just won't go. The gears won't turn. So I end up putting it all right back down in the pile and walking away. It's just... it's exhausting, you know? Trying to force your thoughts into a straight line when they just want to scatter everywhere. So the pile just sits there, getting bigger, because I can't keep my head straight enough to sort it out.
